title: Medical Misinformation and Quality of Public Video Content on Cannabis for Chronic Pain Management: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of the YouTube Platform
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the 66 most-viewed eligible YouTube videos on cannabis for chronic pain (queried 2 August 2022). Two independent reviewers classified every video as useful, misleading, or neither, verifying accuracy against current literature and evidence-based medical-cannabis guidelines; the result is a stated share of items classified misleading (0%, verbatim), with the denominator of 66 videos. The mDISCERN and GQS results are QUALITY measures and recorded as such.

estimates.country: Not stated for the videos (English-language only; the preparatory Google Trends comparison was restricted to the United States)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed cannabis-for-chronic-pain YouTube videos classified as misleading by two clinician-reviewers
estimates.value_raw: 0% of videos were classified as misleading (0 of 66; 15 (22.73%) useful, 51 (77.27%) neither useful nor misleading)
estimates.denominator: 66 videos: the top 150 videos by view count across three searches ('cannabis for pain', 'medical marijuana for pain', 'CBD for pain', 50 each) after excluding videos under one minute, non-English, duplicates, without audio, with fewer than 5,000 views, or unrelated to cannabis for chronic pain
estimates.definition: Video classified misleading if it gave an inaccurate definition of cannabis, at least one inaccurate statement about the pain-reducing mechanism, or at least one inaccurate statement about indications, adverse effects, benefits or outcomes of cannabis for chronic pain; accuracy verified against current literature and published evidence-based guidelines on medical cannabis
estimates.misinfo_def: "The criteria for a video to be deemed misleading were: 1) an inaccurate definition of cannabis, 2) at least one inaccurate statement about the pain-reducing mechanism of cannabis, 3) at least one inaccurate statement about the indications, adverse effects, benefits, and potential outcomes of cannabis for chronic pain management."
estimates.source_quote: Of the total number of videos analyzed, 22.73% (n=15) of videos were classified as useful, 0% of videos were classified as misleading, and 77.27% (n=51) videos were classified as neither useful nor misleading (Table 1).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Video Characteristics and Production Sources', p. 3581; Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers (B.E. and Y.E., medical students/physicians in the author group) applied usefulness criteria drawn from prior systematic reviews, verifying accuracy against current literature and published evidence-based guidelines on medical cannabis. Cohen's kappa between the two reviewers was 0.92 ('almost perfect agreement'), though the Methods attach the kappa computation to the mDISCERN and GQS scores rather than explicitly to the usefulness classification.
estimates.moderator_quote: The results were filtered based on the sort-by-relevance algorithm, and then the videos were filtered by view count from highest to lowest. ... The top 150 videos by view count were selected and screened after the search query.
estimates.notes: A genuine zero-prevalence estimate, stated verbatim, and worth keeping as such: null results are systematically under-reported in this literature. But read it with the authors' own explanation, which an adjudicator needs: 'Interestingly, our search did not capture any videos that were classified as "misleading". We propose several potential explanations... Firstly, our classification criteria for a "misleading" video was likely strict and required false definitions of cannabis, inaccurate descriptions of pain-reducing mechanisms of cannabis, and other non-factual statements. Secondly, our search strategy did not include certain common terms such as "weed".' Note the Discussion describes the misleading criteria as CONJUNCTIVE ('required ... and ...') while the Methods list them as three separate criteria each satisfiable by 'at least one inaccurate statement' — the two readings are not equivalent and the conjunctive one would make a misleading classification near-impossible. Note also that 'neither' is defined as a video containing NO definition, NO mechanism statement and NO statement on indications/effects, yet 77% of videos about cannabis for pain landed there, which suggests the scheme was applied narrowly. denom_selection = curated: view-count-ranked, >=5,000 views, English only. confidence = medium for these reasons, not because the number is unclear.

estimates.country: Not stated for the videos (English-language only)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed cannabis-for-chronic-pain YouTube videos rated low quality (Global Quality Scale < 3)
estimates.value_raw: GQS <3: 18 videos (27.30%) of 66; GQS >=3: 48 (72.70%); mean GQS across all videos 3.05
estimates.definition: Video scored 1 or 2 on the 5-point Global Quality Scale, i.e. poor or generally poor quality with information missing or of limited use to patients
estimates.misinfo_def: "We used the GQS 5-point scoring system to assess the quality of the video content. ... a score of 1 or 2 indicated the video was of low quality, a score of 3 indicated the video was of intermediate quality, and a score of 4 or 5 indicated the video was of good quality."
estimates.source_quote: Video characteristics GQS <3 GQS ≥3 P value Number of videos, N (%) 18 (27.30) 48 (72.70)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Global Quality Scale applied by the same two independent reviewers; Cohen's kappa 0.92 for the mDISCERN and GQS ratings.
estimates.moderator_quote: The videos were assigned a GQS score between 1 and 5, where a score of 1 or 2 indicated the video was of low quality.
estimates.notes: QUALITY construct (clarity, flow, usefulness — not truth), so excluded from prevalence pooling; kept for the appendix. The parallel reliability instrument gives an identical split: mDISCERN <3 = 18 (27.30%), >=3 = 48 (72.70%), mean mDISCERN 3.00. Only one of the two is recorded as a row to avoid duplicating what is effectively the same 18/66 cell.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) The mDISCERN low-reliability share (18/66 = 27.30%, Table 2; mean 3.00) is a second QUALITY measure with the same value as the GQS row and was folded into that row's notes rather than duplicated. 2) Not extracted: the 22.73% useful share (accuracy, not misinformation) and the 77.27% 'neither' share. The Discussion reads the latter as 'suggesting the potential prevalence of less accurate or unnecessary information', but 'neither' is defined by the ABSENCE of any definition/mechanism/indication statement, not by inaccuracy, so it cannot be treated as a misinformation share. 3) Production-source breakdowns (physicians 40% of useful videos, news sources 27.45% of 'neither' videos, physicians 37.50% of GQS>=3 videos, etc.) are compositions of an outcome category, not prevalences, and are subgroup rather than headline results. 4) View counts, likes and comments are engagement means per video with no misinformation numerator, so no EXPOSURE, SHARING or CONCENTRATION row is possible; the paper reports no share of views going to misleading content. 5) No country can be assigned: the videos were not restricted by country and only the Google Trends popularity check was US-scoped. 6) The 44.00% (66/150) inclusion rate is an eligibility funnel, not a content share.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. Search terms chosen after a Google Trends (US, YouTube property, 2019-2022) comparison of 'cannabis', 'marijuana', 'cannabinoids', 'CBD', 'THC'; YouTube queried 2 August 2022 with 'cannabis for pain', 'medical marijuana for pain' and 'CBD for pain'; results sorted by relevance then ranked by view count; top 50 per term (150 screened) reduced to 66 after excluding videos under one minute, non-English, duplicates, without audio, with fewer than 5,000 views, or off-topic (44.0% inclusion). Two independent reviewers extracted metadata and classified each video useful / misleading / neither against current literature and published medical-cannabis guidelines, and scored the 5-item mDISCERN and the 5-point GQS. Cohen's kappa between reviewers 0.92. Comparisons by t-test and chi-square, alpha 0.05. Authors' stated limits: single time point, English only, YouTube only, search terms omitted colloquialisms such as 'weed', and the misleading criteria were probably too strict.
